question: Tell me about a situation where miscommunication caused a problem. How did you resolve it and prevent recurrence?

raiseTranscript.text: On my first project, I misunderstood the acceptance criteria for a feature and built the wrong flow. The PM caught it in review.
What exactly was miscommunicated?
The ticket said 'support mobile' but I took it as responsive web only. I assumed the backend changes were out of scope.
How did you fix it and stop it happening again?
I rewrote the module in two days. After that I started asking the PM to confirm scope in a quick chat before starting any ticket.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a situation where miscommunication caused a problem. How did you resolve it and prevent recurrence?
Situation: Misread 'support mobile' as responsive web only
Action: Rewrote module; started pre-work confirmation chat with PM
Outcome: Feature shipped on revised timeline
Quote: 'I started asking the PM to confirm scope in a quick chat before starting any ticket'
Follow-up: How did the team react? 'PM appreciated it and it became our default for new hires'
junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for junior. The candidate owned the misread requirement and implemented a lightweight personal process to confirm scope before coding. Quote shows they turned the incident into a repeatable habit rather than a one-off apology. Story stays within individual scope, which is appropriate. Biggest strength is the simple, sustainable prevention step that demonstrates coachability.

lowerTranscript.text: The designer sent specs late and the build was wrong. I had to stay late to fix it.
What was the actual miscommunication?
They didn't tell me the colors were final. I used placeholders.
What did you change to prevent it next time?
I just waited for them to message me instead of starting early.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a situation where miscommunication caused a problem. How did you resolve it and prevent recurrence?
Situation: Designer specs arrived late, colors not marked final
Action: Stayed late to fix; shifted to waiting for designer messages
Outcome: No change in process or shared understanding
Quote: 'I just waited for them to message me instead of starting early'
Follow-up: Did you talk to the designer? 'No, I just stopped starting early'
junior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for junior. Candidate attributes the problem entirely to the designer and adopts a passive workaround instead of seeking clarity. No evidence of learning a repeatable communication habit. Story shows avoidance rather than ownership. Biggest gap is lack of any proactive step to close the information gap in future work.

raiseTranscript.text: Two platform teams had different assumptions about a shared API contract. One side shipped a breaking change that broke three downstream services.
How did you surface and fix the misalignment?
I wrote a one-page contract diff and ran a 30-minute sync with both leads. We agreed on versioning and published it in the shared repo.
What prevented recurrence?
We added an automated contract test in CI and required sign-off from both teams before any change. Downtime dropped to zero on subsequent releases.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a situation where miscommunication caused a problem. How did you resolve it and prevent recurrence?
Situation: Two platform teams shipped breaking API change
Action: Created contract diff, ran cross-team sync, added CI contract test + dual sign-off
Outcome: Zero downtime on later releases
Quote: 'We added an automated contract test in CI and required sign-off from both teams'
Follow-up: How did you get the second team to agree? 'I showed the three broken services and let the data drive the discussion'
senior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for senior. Candidate drove resolution across two teams without authority by using data and a lightweight process change. The prevention step (CI test + dual sign-off) shows influence that lasted beyond the incident. Quote ties the action directly to measurable stability improvement. Biggest strength is converting a one-time fix into a durable cross-team mechanism.

lowerTranscript.text: Marketing and engineering disagreed on launch timing and the email went out before the feature was ready.
What did you do to resolve it?
I sent a long email explaining the correct order.
Did anything change for the next launch?
We just made sure to include more people on the thread.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a situation where miscommunication caused a problem. How did you resolve it and prevent recurrence?
Situation: Marketing email sent before feature ready
Action: Sent explanatory email; added more people to thread
Outcome: No structural change
Quote: 'We just made sure to include more people on the thread'
Follow-up: Did you create any shared artifact or process? 'No, just the bigger email list'
senior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for senior. Candidate relied on a single email and broader distribution rather than creating shared clarity or a repeatable checkpoint. No evidence of cross-team influence or lasting process improvement. Story remains reactive. Biggest gap is absence of any mechanism that would have prevented the same misalignment on future launches.

raiseTranscript.text: My team and the data platform team kept missing handoff details on a metrics migration. Three releases had incorrect dashboards.
How did you address the recurring issue?
I paired an engineer from each team for a two-week shadow period and created a joint runbook. I also started a weekly 15-minute sync between the two tech leads.
What was the result on team performance?
Error rate on handoffs fell from 40% to under 5%. The runbook is now used by both teams for any shared work.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a situation where miscommunication caused a problem. How did you resolve it and prevent recurrence?
Situation: Recurring incorrect dashboards between two teams
Action: Instituted paired shadowing, joint runbook, weekly lead sync
Outcome: Handoff error rate 40% -> <5%; runbook adopted broadly
Quote: 'The runbook is now used by both teams for any shared work'
Follow-up: How did you handle resistance from the other manager? 'I framed it as reducing their on-call load and let the leads own the runbook'
manager.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for manager. Candidate used team-level levers (shadowing, runbook, recurring sync) to reduce recurring errors rather than heroic individual fixes. The 40% to <5% drop shows ownership of team outcomes. Quote demonstrates the change became self-sustaining across teams. Biggest strength is building leverage through process instead of repeated intervention.

lowerTranscript.text: My team kept getting requirements late from product. I told them to ask more questions.
Did you change how the teams worked together?
I added it to the retro notes and reminded people in standup.
Any measurable change?
Not really, we still miss things sometimes.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a situation where miscommunication caused a problem. How did you resolve it and prevent recurrence?
Situation: Late requirements from product
Action: Told team to ask more questions; added to retro and standup reminders
Outcome: No measurable improvement
Quote: 'Not really, we still miss things sometimes'
Follow-up: Did you engage the product manager directly? 'Only through the retro notes'
manager.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for manager. Candidate delegated the problem back to the team without creating any structural change or engaging the partner team. No evidence of using manager authority to build durable coordination. Story shows reminders rather than leverage. Biggest gap is lack of ownership for cross-team outcomes.

raiseTranscript.text: Sales and product had fundamentally different views on which customer segment we were optimizing for, leading to a six-month delay on a major initiative.
What did you do at the org level?

I created a quarterly segment-alignment forum with sales, product, and finance leads and required every new initiative to include a one-page segment hypothesis signed by all three. We also tied part of the sales incentive to validated segment data instead of just closed deals.
What was the longer-term impact?
Initiative cycle time dropped 30% and we stopped re-litigating the same segment debates in every planning cycle.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a situation where miscommunication caused a problem. How did you resolve it and prevent recurrence?
Situation: Six-month delay from sales/product segment misalignment
Action: Quarterly alignment forum + signed segment hypothesis + incentive redesign
Outcome: 30% faster initiative cycle time; eliminated repeated debates
Quote: 'We tied part of the sales incentive to validated segment data instead of just closed deals'
Follow-up: How did you get sales leadership to accept the incentive change? 'I showed the revenue impact of the six-month delay and let finance co-own the metric'
exec.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for exec. Candidate addressed root misalignment through structural changes (forum, required hypothesis, incentive redesign) rather than case-by-case resolution. The 30% cycle-time improvement reflects org-level leverage. Quote shows willingness to change incentives to align behavior. Biggest strength is converting a painful delay into durable governance that removed recurring friction.

lowerTranscript.text: Different teams had different priorities and projects slipped. I started sending a weekly priority email to all VPs.
Did the pattern of slips change?
Some teams read it, others didn't. We still have to escalate case by case.
Any systemic fix?
We talk about it in the monthly all-hands.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a situation where miscommunication caused a problem. How did you resolve it and prevent recurrence?
Situation: Priority misalignment across teams causing slips
Action: Weekly priority email to VPs; monthly all-hands mention
Outcome: Continued case-by-case escalations
Quote: 'We still have to escalate case by case'
Follow-up: Did you change any decision rights or forums? 'No, just the email and all-hands'
exec.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for exec. Candidate relied on broadcast communication without altering decision rights, incentives, or forums. No evidence of strategic trade-off or org redesign to prevent recurrence. Story remains at the level of reminders. Biggest gap is absence of leverage that would scale beyond the candidate's personal involvement.

30% cycle-time improvement and eliminated recurring debates

diagnostic.exec: Co-owned metric with finance to shift sales incentives
